Dynamic factor models

Nicholas J Clark

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/dfm.Rmd
dfm.Rmd

Series measured together often move together. Sites in one habitat share weather. Species in one guild share resource pulses. A dynamic factor model describes that common variation with a small number of latent trends. It writes each series as a weighted sum of them (Zuur et al. 2003; Holmes et al. 2012). In mvgam the trend_map argument sets which series load on which trend. This vignette simulates six series from three trends and fits three models: one given the true loadings, one that estimates them and one that pools every series onto a single trend. Forecast scores on held-out data then compare the three.

The model

For series \(j\) and latent trend \(k\), the mean of each series on the link scale is a linear combination of the trends:

\[\begin{align*} y_{j, t} & \sim F(\mu_{j, t}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \\ g(\mu_{j, t}) & = \beta_0 + \beta^\top \mathbf{x}_{j, t} + \sum_{k = 1}^{N_{lv}} Z_{j, k} \, z_{k, t} \\ z_{k, t} & \sim \text{AR}(1) \text{ or any other trend model} \end{align*}\]

\(Z\) is the loading matrix, with one row per series and one column per trend. Row \(j\) gives the weight of each trend in series \(j\). Every series with a non-zero weight on trend \(k\) uses the same latent path \(z_{k, 1:T}\). All of those series inform its posterior. With fewer trends than series, the model reduces the dimension of the problem.

Three ways to write trend_map

trend_map supplies \(Z\) in one of three forms:

  • A keyword. "identity" gives each series its own trend. "shared" gives every series the same trend.
  • A data.frame with columns series and trend. Series given the same trend number share that trend with a loading of one.
  • A numeric matrix with one row per series and one column per trend. mvgam holds each number fixed and estimates each NA.

The matrix form covers partial knowledge. Here five series have known loadings and the fifth series is free to load on any of three trends:

Z_partial <- rbind(
  s1 = c(1, 0, 0),
  s2 = c(1, 0, 0),
  s3 = c(1, 0, 0),
  s4 = c(0, 1, 0),
  s5 = c(NA, NA, NA),
  s6 = c(0, 0, 1)
)

Passed as trend_map = Z_partial, the fit estimates the three NA entries. summary() lists them under Factor Loadings. A matrix of all NA estimates every loading, as shown later in this vignette.

Simulated data

To compare the three models with known loadings, we simulated six series from three AR(1) trends. Trend 1 is strongly autocorrelated (\(\phi_1 = 0.85\)) and drives series 1 to 3. Trend 2 is weakly autocorrelated (\(\phi_2 = 0.15\)) and drives series 4 and 5. Trend 3 (\(\phi_3 = 0.55\)) has the largest innovation SD and drives series 6 alone. The last 15 of the 80 time points are held out.

set.seed(3)

n_time <- 80
n_series <- 6
n_lv <- 3
n_train <- 65
phi_true <- c(0.85, 0.15, 0.55)
sig_true <- c(0.5, 0.35, 0.8)

# Each trend starts at its stationary distribution
lv <- matrix(NA, n_time, n_lv)
lv[1, ] <- rnorm(n_lv, 0, sig_true / sqrt(1 - phi_true^2))
for (t in 2:n_time) {
  lv[t, ] <- phi_true * lv[t - 1L, ] + rnorm(n_lv, 0, sig_true)
}

# Series 1-3 load on trend 1, series 4-5 on trend 2, series 6 on trend 3
Z_true <- matrix(0, nrow = n_series, ncol = n_lv)
Z_true[cbind(1:6, c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3))] <- 1

# Observations add Gaussian noise with SD 0.2
y_mat <- lv %*% t(Z_true) +
  matrix(rnorm(n_time * n_series, 0, 0.2), n_time, n_series)

sim_data <- data.frame(
  time = rep(seq_len(n_time), n_series),
  series = factor(
    rep(paste0("s", seq_len(n_series)), each = n_time),
    levels = paste0("s", seq_len(n_series))
  ),
  y = as.numeric(y_mat)
)
train <- sim_data[sim_data$time <= n_train, ]
test  <- sim_data[sim_data$time >  n_train, ]

mvgam_data() checks the training data and plots each series, with the held-out points in black:

mvgam_data(train, family = gaussian(), trend_formula = ~ AR(),
           newdata = test)

The six simulated series. Series 1 to 3 follow one trend, series 4 and 5 a second, and series 6 a third. Black points after the dashed line are held out.

Fitting known loadings

The first model is given the true grouping as a data.frame:

tm_known <- data.frame(
  series = paste0("s", seq_len(n_series)),
  trend = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 3L)
)
tm_known
#>   series trend
#> 1     s1     1
#> 2     s2     1
#> 3     s3     1
#> 4     s4     2
#> 5     s5     2
#> 6     s6     3

The observation formula holds an intercept alone. AR(p = 1) gives each of the three trends its own AR(1) process. Passing newdata = test stores the held-out data on the fit for forecast() to use later.

fit_known <- mvgam(
  formula = y ~ 1,
  trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
  trend_map = tm_known,
  data = train,
  newdata = test,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 2L,
  iter = 1000L,
  warmup = 500L,
  silent = 2L
)
summary(fit_known)

summary() reports one AR coefficient and one innovation SD per trend. The 95% intervals of all six parameters contain the simulated values. The observation SD is estimated at its true value of 0.2.

plot(type = "factors") draws each latent trend with the share of the series-level variance it explains. Because three of the six series load on it, trend 1 explains the most. Trend 3 drives one series and comes second, as its innovations are the largest.

plot(fit_known, type = "factors")

The three latent trends of the model given the true loadings, each labelled with the share of series-level variance it explains.

forecast() extends each trend over the held-out times and maps the draws back to the series through \(Z\). Series on the same trend receive the same latent forecast. The forecast for the weakly autocorrelated trend returns to its mean within a few steps. The forecast for the strongly autocorrelated trend returns slowly.

fc_known <- forecast(fit_known)
plot(fc_known)

Forecasts from the model given the true loadings. Points are observations, and those after the dashed line were held out.

Estimating the loadings

When the grouping is unknown, a matrix of NA asks mvgam to estimate every loading. The loadings take a Student-t prior. The innovation SD of every factor is fixed at one to set the scale of the loadings. Because each factor has its own AR coefficient, the model distinguishes the factors by their dynamics. Only their order and signs are arbitrary. mvgam orders the factors by the variance they explain and gives each a positive largest loading.

fit_free <- mvgam(
  formula = y ~ 1,
  trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
  trend_map = matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_series, ncol = n_lv),
  data = train,
  newdata = test,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 2L,
  iter = 1000L,
  warmup = 500L,
  silent = 2L
)
summary(fit_free)

summary() reports the loading of every series on every factor, where Z[i, k] is the loading of series i on factor k. Series 1 to 3 load on the first factor and series 6 on the second. Series 4 and 5 load on the third. The 95% intervals of all other loadings contain zero. The model recovered the simulated grouping without being given it. The interval of each AR coefficient contains the simulated value of the trend its factor matches.

plot(fit_free, type = "factors")

The three latent factors of the model that estimates its loadings. Factors 1, 2 and 3 match trends 1, 3 and 2 of the simulation.

Each factor explains a similar share of the variance as its trend does in the model given the true loadings.

The dependence among series is often the target of a factor model. residual_cor() computes the correlations that the loadings imply between each pair of series:

plot(residual_cor(fit_free))

Posterior median correlations among the six series, implied by the estimated loadings.

The correlations show the same grouping. Series 1 to 3 are strongly correlated with one another, as are series 4 and 5. Series 6 is weakly correlated with the rest.

ordinate() shows the same structure as a biplot. Each arrow is the loading of one series on the first two factors. Each numbered point is a time. Series that share a trend point in the same direction.

ordinate(fit_free)

Ordination of the model that estimates its loadings. Arrows are series loadings on the first two factors, and numbered points are times.

Pooling every series

To see what a wrong grouping costs, the third model puts all six series on one trend with trend_map = "shared":

fit_pooled <- mvgam(
  formula = y ~ 1,
  trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
  trend_map = "shared",
  data = train,
  newdata = test,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 2L,
  iter = 1000L,
  warmup = 500L,
  silent = 2L
)
fc_pooled <- forecast(fit_pooled)
plot(fc_pooled)

Forecasts from the model that pools all six series onto one trend. The intervals over the training period are much wider than those of the model given the true loadings.

One trend cannot follow three different sets of dynamics. The model assigns the remaining variation to observation noise. Its intervals over the training period are several times wider than those of the first model.

Comparing forecasts

compare_scores() scores the three forecasts against the held-out data. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and the log score are computed for each series and horizon. The energy score is computed across all series at each horizon. Lower values are better for all three. The chunk below sums each score over the held-out period.

fc_free <- forecast(fit_free)
total_score <- function(score) {
  by_horizon <- summary(compare_scores(
    fc_known, fc_free, fc_pooled,
    score = score, model_names = c("known", "free", "pooled")
  ))
  colSums(by_horizon[, c("known", "free", "pooled")])
}
totals <- sapply(c("crps", "logs", "energy"), total_score)
round(totals, 1)
#>        crps  logs energy
#> known  38.2  92.6   19.5
#> free   38.7  94.8   19.8
#> pooled 41.4 110.9   20.5

The pooled model has the worst total on all three scores. Its log score of 110.9 compares with 92.6 for the model given the true loadings. The model that estimates its loadings scores 38.7 on CRPS and 94.8 on the log score, close to the 38.2 and 92.6 of the model given the true loadings. In this simulation, estimating the loadings cost little forecast accuracy. A wrong grouping cost much more.

A held-out forecast score is a practical check on a proposed grouping. Where two candidate trend_map structures are plausible, fit both and compare their scores.

Where to next

  • ?mvgam describes trend_map and loadings_prior, which sets a structured prior on estimated loadings.
  • ?compare_scores and ?score list the available scoring rules.
  • ?residual_cor and ?shared_variation give the correlations and covariances among series, with their intervals.
  • ?ordinate describes the biplot. ?active_factors helps choose the number of factors.
  • how_to_cite() writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model with the references for its factor structure. methods_md() writes out its equations.
  • The forecast evaluation article covers lfo_cv() and ensemble() for comparing and combining models.
  • The JSDM article applies the same factor structure to community data with jsdgam().
  • The VAR article covers models where each series keeps its own trend and the trends affect one another.
  • The overview vignette introduces the other trend models and their arguments.

References

Heaps, S. E. and Jermyn, I. H. (2024). Structured prior distributions for the covariance matrix in latent factor models. Statistics and Computing 34, 143. doi:10.1007/s11222-024-10454-0

Holmes, E. E., Ward, E. J. and Wills, K. (2012). MARSS: Multivariate Autoregressive State-space Models for Analyzing Time-series Data. The R Journal 4(1), 11-19. doi:10.32614/RJ-2012-002

Zuur, A. F., Fryer, R. J., Jolliffe, I. T., Dekker, R. and Beukema, J. J. (2003). Estimating common trends in multivariate time series using dynamic factor analysis. Environmetrics 14(7), 665-685. doi:10.1002/env.611
